ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Bruce Lee — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Urgent follow-up four days after an emergency visit for a first convulsive collapse: history from him and a witness, triggers, examination, ECG, laboratory tests, driving and seizure safety, cannabis counseling, chronic back pain, and urgent epilepsy referral

text.paragraph: Urgent follow-up four days after an emergency visit for a first convulsive collapse: history from him and a witness, triggers, examination, ECG, laboratory tests, driving and seizure safety, cannabis counseling, chronic back pain, and urgent epilepsy referral [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He wants to know what happened and whether it will happen again, and to keep training and making films. [S]
He does not want a daily medicine unless it is clearly needed, and wants to understand the evidence and decide for himself. [S]
His back pain must not stop him training. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Bruce Jun Fan Lee was born on November 27, 1940, at the Jackson Street Hospital in San Francisco's Chinatown, while his parents were on tour with the Chinese opera; his parents named him Jun Fan, and a nurse at the hospital gave him the English name Bruce. At three months old he returned with his parents to Hong Kong, where he was raised until the age of 18. [D]
His Chinese name was 李振藩 (Lee Jun-fan in Cantonese romanization); as a child actor he took the stage name 李小龍 (Lee Siu-lung, "Little Dragon"). [D]
Raised in Hong Kong, he was a child actor in some 20 films; at 13 he began studying wing chun gung fu under Yip Man, and he was also an accomplished dancer. [D]

In 1959 he returned to the United States, settled in Seattle, studied philosophy at the University of Washington and began teaching gung fu, opening schools in Seattle, Oakland and Los Angeles; he developed his own martial art, Jeet Kune Do ("the way of the intercepting fist"), grounded in simplicity, directness and personal freedom. He is known for the words "Be water, my friend." [D]

In 1970, without warming up, he lifted a 125-pound barbell in a "good morning" exercise and severely injured his back; after many tests an injury to the fourth sacral nerve was found. He was ordered to complete bed rest, told he would never do gung fu again, and stayed in bed for about six months before beginning his own recovery program; the injury became a chronic source of pain for the rest of his life. [D]

He returned to Hong Kong to make films for Golden Harvest: The Big Boss (1971), Fist of Fury and The Way of the Dragon, which he wrote, directed and starred in; Enter the Dragon, the first Hong Kong and Hollywood co-production, was released after his death. [D]

On May 10, 1973, while dubbing lines for Enter the Dragon at Golden Harvest's Hammer Hill Road studios in Hong Kong, he felt faint, collapsed in the bathroom, was helped back to the dubbing studio, vomited and fainted again; he was taken to hospital in critical condition, where a neurosurgeon diagnosed cerebral oedema and gave mannitol to reduce the swelling. He recovered. [D]

His biographer Matthew Polly, as quoted in the Clinical Kidney Journal, wrote that on May 10 "his body began convulsing" after he lost consciousness; a seizure was considered a potential cause of the episode, but because it was a single episode, epilepsy was not diagnosed. [D]

The air conditioning in the dubbing room had been turned off to avoid sound problems in the recording, and he had high temperature, weakness, vomiting and loss of consciousness, according to his biographer. [D]
He had used cannabis (hashish) on the day of the May 10 collapse; the Hong Kong neurosurgeon who treated him thought it was a factor, an explanation he rejected. [D]
His biographer reported that some months before May 1973 he had the sweat glands removed from his armpits. [D]

He married in 1964; a son was born in 1965 and a daughter in 1969. His father, the Cantonese opera performer and actor Lee Hoi Chuen, died in Hong Kong in 1965, a week after the birth of his first grandchild. [D]

list.item: Sudden collapse with loss of consciousness four days before the visit, after hours of voice recording in a hot booth with the air conditioning off: felt hot and faint, lost consciousness, generalized stiffening then jerking of all four limbs for about a minute, vomiting, and 20 to 30 minutes of confusion; seizure versus convulsive syncope; emergency evaluation the same day: active, provisional [S]

Chronic low back pain since a weightlifting injury three years ago, reported as an injury to a sacral nerve; worse with long sitting and heavy lifting; no weakness, numbness or bladder or bowel change: active, confirmed [S]

Culturally appropriate care: ask how he wishes to be addressed and in which language; explain the evidence plainly and let him decide; respect his own training methods and philosophy; share information with his family only as he chooses. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015) [S]

Urgent referral to the epilepsy clinic within the week, with MRI of the brain with an epilepsy protocol and a sleep-deprived EEG. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015); Practice Parameter: evaluating an apparent unprovoked first seizure in adults (an evidence-based review) (2007) [S]

Laboratory tests after the seizure: sodium, glucose, calcium, magnesium, kidney function, creatine kinase, blood count and TSH, with creatine kinase and creatinine repeated until normal. Guideline: Practice Parameter: evaluating an apparent unprovoked first seizure in adults (an evidence-based review) (2007) [S]

No driving until the epilepsy clinic has seen him and the period without seizures it advises has passed; Hong Kong's driving licence regulations list epilepsy and liability to sudden fainting among the conditions for which the Commissioner for Transport must refuse or cancel a licence. Guideline: Supplementary Health Information Sheet for Driver Assessment (First Schedule of the Road Traffic (Driving Licences) Regulations, Cap. 374B) (2021); Neurological disorders: assessing fitness to drive (first unprovoked epileptic seizure) (2026) [S]

Seizure safety: no swimming alone, no work at heights or with dangerous machinery, showers rather than baths, and seizure first aid taught to the people he works with; a stunt double for falls and heights until the clinic advises otherwise. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015); First Aid for Seizures (2024) [S]

Triggers: at least seven hours of sleep, regular meals, breaks and air conditioning during long recording and training sessions, and drinking to thirst with salty food or an electrolyte drink in the heat rather than large volumes of plain water. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015) [S]

Cannabis: a nonjudgmental conversation about cannabis, heat, sleep loss and seizures; he chose to stop while his risk is highest; no synthetic cannabinoids. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015) [S]

Medicine safety: avoid medicines that lower the seizure threshold, such as tramadol, bupropion and high doses of sedating antihistamines, and sedatives whose withdrawal can provoke seizures, such as meprobamate and carisoprodol; tell any doctor or pharmacist about the seizure. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015); Noninvasive Treatments for Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Low Back Pain: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians (2017) [S]

Chronic back pain: a structured core strengthening and motor control program with a physical therapist, heat, and acetaminophen when needed; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs only in short courses, with food and normal fluids; no opioids. Guideline: Noninvasive Treatments for Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Low Back Pain: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians (2017) [S]
Referral to neurology (epilepsy), Priyanka Abernathy-Leung, MD, ordered 1973-05-14 [S]
